summary:
The STOP CCP Act (H.R. 3334) establishes a mandatory sanctions regime targeting specified Chinese Communist Party officials, successor-organization officials, adult family members, and certain Chinese state-owned enterprises involved in fentanyl activity. Sections 2 and 3 set forth congressional findings and a sense of Congress concerning Hong Kong autonomy, Taiwan, Xinjiang, Tibet-related human rights issues, and related conduct by the Chinese Communist Party.

Section 4(a) requires the President, not later than 30 days after enactment, to impose the sanctions described in § 4(c) on: (1) each member, including alternate members, of the Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party whom the President determines engages in sanctionable conduct under § 4(b); (2) each member of any successor organization, if the Central Committee is dissolved, who engages in such conduct; (3) each adult family member, including a spouse or adult family member of the spouse, of such a person; and (4) each person the President determines is a Chinese state-owned enterprise illegally manufacturing or distributing fentanyl, or knowingly or intentionally manufacturing or distributing fentanyl precursor chemicals for illegal fentanyl production or distribution. Section 4(b) defines sanctionable conduct as playing a significant role in developing or implementing government policies or laws that the President determines appear designed to violate Hong Kong autonomy, harass or increase aggression toward Taiwan, contribute to political oppression or human rights violations within China, including Uyghur Muslims, or willfully and knowingly engage in malicious activities, including online disinformation and propaganda, to interfere with U.S. Federal, State, or local elections.

Section 4(c) requires blocking of property and interests in property under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), 50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq., when within U.S. jurisdiction or U.S.-person control, and imposes visa, admission, parole, and Immigration and Nationality Act benefit ineligibility, with mandatory visa revocation under INA § 221(i), 8 U.S.C. 1201(i). Exceptions apply for compliance with the U.N. Headquarters Agreement or other applicable international obligations, and for authorized U.S. intelligence, law enforcement, or national security activities.

Section 4(d) applies IEEPA civil and criminal penalties under 50 U.S.C. 1705(b)–(c) to violations. Sections 4(e) and 4(f) authorize use of IEEPA §§ 203 and 205, 50 U.S.C. 1702 and 1704, and require implementing regulations within 30 days. Section 4(g) authorizes renewable waivers of up to 60 days upon 15 days’ prior certification to specified congressional committees that the waiver is vital to U.S. national security. Section 4(h) permits termination of sanctions after congressional certification and public posting, based either on specified cessation of conduct by the PRC and CCP or specified remedial action by the sanctioned person. Section 4(i) sunsets the President’s waiver and license authorities with respect to required sanctions two years after enactment. Section 4(j) excludes sanctions on importation of goods. The bill contains no authorization of appropriations.
